title: Form and Meaning in Verse
text:
Translators of poetry face a dilemma that prose translators rarely encounter. The rhyme scheme and metre of a sonnet are often as integral to its meaning as its vocabulary, so a faithful rendering of content may sacrifice form entirely. Many translators therefore accept a looser fidelity, aiming to reproduce the emotional effect rather than each syllable.

Critics who prize strict equivalence argue that such freedom amounts to a second, invented poem. Their opponents reply that poetry translated without recreating its music is merely a dictionary entry, and that the translator's task is to recreate the poem as a living object in another tongue. Neither position is wholly convincing, which is why the debate has endured for centuries.

questions.text: According to the passage, why do poetry translators face a dilemma that prose translators rarely encounter?
options: Poems are always longer than prose texts.
A poem's rhyme scheme and metre are often integral to its meaning.
Poetry is never translated into other languages.
Publishers pay poets less than prose writers.

questions.text: What do critics who prize strict equivalence argue about greater translator freedom?
options: It produces a more accurate dictionary.
It amounts to a second, invented poem.
It always improves the original text.

questions.text: What can be inferred about a translator who aims at emotional effect?
options: They reject the emotional content of the poem.
They accept some loss of exact form to preserve the poem's impact.

questions.text: The passage suggests that the debate has lasted for centuries mainly because:
options: translators are rarely paid for their work.
neither position fully resolves the tension between form and meaning.
poets refuse to allow any translations.

vocabulary.definition: the quality of staying faithful to an original
the regular rhythmic pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in verse
essential and necessary to make a whole complete
a state of being equal in value, meaning or effect

paragraph_translations: Tłumacze poezji stają przed dylematem, z którym rzadko mierzą się tłumacze prozy. Schemat rymów i metrum sonetu bywa tak samo integralną częścią znaczenia jak jego słownictwo, więc wierne oddanie treści może oznaczać całkowite poświęcenie formy. Wielu tłumaczy dlatego przyjmuje mniej dosłowną wierność, dążąc do odtworzenia emocjonalnego efektu, a nie każdej sylaby.

Krytycy ceniący ścisły ekwiwalent twierdzą, że taka swoboda oznacza drugi, wymyślony wiersz. Ich przeciwnicy odpowiadają, że poezja przełożona bez odtworzenia nowej muzyki to tylko hasło słownikowe, a zadaniem tłumacza jest odtworzenie wiersza jako żywego tworu w innym języku. Żadne z tych stanowisk nie jest w pełni przekonujące, dlatego spór trwa od wieków.
